doc.title: Larry Ridley interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 10, 2003

title: Good ears, learning tunes and composing solos; Giant Steps and Sonny Stitt story
summary: Students must learn melodies and the blues before Giant Steps; solos should be composed with structure, and Dorham, Parker and Jackson advised stopping early.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: having good ears. You know because when you’re up there improvising you’re not thinking about oh I’m going from a D minor seventh with a flat five over here to a G seven with a raised nine. You’re not thinking about all that. You’ve got to sit at the piano and you’ve got to get that sound, or the guitar, and get those sounds in your ear and know how to respond to that improvisationally through hearing lyrical lines. And that’s one of the things I’m concerned about that is happening with jazz education. Too many of these kids are coming through and they sound like computers because they’re learning how to play licks and patterns but they’re not learning how get their own personal sound. And that’s what jazz is all about, finding your own identity. I don’t try to play the bass like Ray Brown or Paul Chambers or Richard Davis or any — Charlie Mingus. You know? I have learned how to be Larry Ridley. Because — as the Bible says, to thine own self be true. Of course I’ve learned from them and there are certain things that I have picked up from them but I don’t try to just say oh, that’s not the way Ray played it so I’ve got to go back and try that again. It’s not about that.
How can you foster that ability to invent melodies and what happened to you with this — being thrown in that situation? How can we do that now?

They’ve got to learn tunes. The more songs that you know that have melodic content — the brain is like a computer. You have to — if you put garbage in you’re going to get garbage out. So you have to put something up there. And one of the things that I always stress to my students when they’re in the workshops and things I do, how many melodies do you know? I’ve done artists-in-residencies in different places. I will never forget one time I was at the University of Utah. I asked the young people what do they want to play. They says let’s play “Giant Steps.” I said, “Excuse me?” Okay. Blues in B flat. They said, “But we said we want to play ‘Giant Steps.’” I said, “No, you have to show me that you can play the Blues in B flat, or any key for that matter, before you can talk about ‘Giant Steps,’” I said, “because I came up around John Coltrane. John Coltrane, see you all come in at these different stages of hearing people. And see Coltrane is so beautiful because his career is documented on recordings. You can hear the growth. See all that stuff that he was playing at the end, he could still go back and walk the bar, which is the basic stuff in the community.” I remember a woman coming up to Sonny Stitt, he came through Indianapolis playing at this club and he was up there just taking it easy because he thought well I’m in Indianapolis I’ll just kind of take it easy. This woman came up to him and she says, “Sonny Stitt, let me tell you something. I spent my last five dollars to come in here to hear you play because I like your music.” She said, “But you better stop bullshitting on that stage or I’m going to take one of these chairs and go upside your head.” So he said, “Oh, excuse me, madam” and commenced to bear down and start playing. And it’s that kind of thing. You know like but they have to know melodies. They
have to learn tunes. They’re learning too many things like exercises that take you through the two-five-one progression. Or I’m going to play the Dorian or the Lydiot or Idiot scale.

Or the demented scale. And they have to understand that you’re composing music. And you have to relate to your audience. Nobody wants to come and hear you practice. I don’t want to come and hear you sit up and play exercises. I mean do that in your house or in your practice room or something like that. You have to learn how to compose music. That’s the beauty of jazz. You’re called upon to be an instantaneous composer. You have to learn how to build your solos. I hear these kids, they’re just playing ad infinitum. Well let me show you everything I’ve practiced today. No. That’s not music. When you listen to Bach, Beethoven, any of those European art music masters it’s just like writing — that’s why I always compare it to English composition even. You know you have to have an introduction, you introduce your theme, your thesis, you develop it, you recapitulate, you do a summarization and then you lock up and bow as Kenny Dorham used to say. Kenny used to say, “Get two choruses of your best shit together baby, and lock up and bow out.” And Charlie Parker used to say, “It’s always best to leave people wanting more.” And Milt Jackson used to tell me, “Once you get past the third chorus you’re practicing.”
